entry.title: DeepMind introduces AlphaProof Code, an AI system that generated three million lines of formal proofs in Lean to verify Signal's core encryption [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DeepMind has developed AlphaProof Code, an AI agent capable of producing extensive formal proofs to verify complex software systems. The system wrote three million lines of proofs in the Lean theorem prover to validate the security of Signal's core encryption. This breakthrough demonstrates the potential of AI to assist in deep software verification tasks, improving the reliability and security of critical cryptographic software. The approach could pave the way for more automated and rigorous software assurance in security-sensitive applications.

entry.title: VulnCheck tracks 442 CVEs attributed to Anthropic's Project Glasswing with only two exploited in the wild, revealing a widening gap between vulnerability discovery and fixes
entry.summary: VulnCheck has monitored Anthropic's Project Glasswing for seven months, identifying 442 CVEs linked to the project, which represents about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year. Despite nearly 38,000 reported findings, only 7,349 have been made public and just 217 fixed, with only two vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, raising questions about the project's impact and effectiveness. Since September, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 new findings but fixed only 15, while duplicates and withdrawn findings have increased significantly, suggesting challenges in managing and remediating reported vulnerabilities. Anthropic's claimed true positive rate has risen to 94.2%, but external validation, such as from the curl project, has disputed many reported vulnerabilities, further complicating the assessment of the project's accuracy and value.

entry.title: Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and MDN teams launch Modern Web Guidance to help coding agents adopt modern web platform features over legacy JavaScript patterns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Modern Web Guidance is a collaborative project by Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams that provides curated skills and best practices to steer coding agents away from outdated JavaScript toward modern web platform APIs. It offers a CLI tool that integrates expert guidance on browser compatibility, performance, accessibility, and native web features to improve code quality and efficiency. The guidance covers recent web platform advancements including CSS layout, animations, native UI components, accessibility improvements, and built-in AI capabilities like on-device language detection and translation. It aims to reduce reliance on legacy code and heavy polyfills by promoting lightweight, platform-optimized solutions. The project includes tools to scan codebases for legacy patterns and retrieve targeted modernization advice, supporting developers in producing production-ready, modern web applications.

entry.title: Engineer warns AI-generated codebases tend to be fragile due to shallow tests, complexity, reduced human understanding, and rapid changes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A former Meta engineer who transitioned to fully AI-generated coding at a large tech company highlights that AI-assisted development often produces brittle codebases. The engineer notes that AI tends to write superficial tests, overly complex code, and accelerates development pace beyond human review capacity, leading to increased technical debt and fragility. The engineer identifies four main issues with AI-generated code: shallow test coverage that misses critical cases, unnecessary complexity from rigid adherence to coding guidelines, diminished human understanding of the codebase, and faster pull requests that reduce review quality. These factors contribute to more frequent and prolonged incidents in production environments, raising concerns about the sustainability of AI-driven software development for large-scale SaaS applications.

entry.title: Researcher explains reasoning in AI as pathfinding through token space, clarifying why longer chains of thought do not always improve accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The article presents a perspective on reasoning in AI models as a process of pathfinding through token space, where multiple paths can lead from a prompt to a correct answer. It challenges the intuitive idea that longer chains of thought always yield better results, noting that forcing longer reasoning chains can sometimes degrade accuracy. Instead, reasoning success depends on the probability of sampling paths that reach correct answers, which can be improved by training models to generate better paths or by sampling multiple paths and selecting the best. The author illustrates this concept with examples and mathematical formulations, explaining how reinforcement learning maximizes the likelihood of finding successful paths rather than guaranteeing convergence on a single chain. This framework also helps explain phenomena like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking in reasoning models. The article suggests that increasing the number of sampled reasoning paths is a more reliable way to improve accuracy than simply extending the length of individual reasoning chains.

entry.title: ZeroPoint introduces a fixed zero-energy state in energy-based decision models to enable explicit abstention decisions, improving option compatibility assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ZeroPoint is a new energy-based model (EBM) that assigns a fixed zero energy to an empty answer state for every input, providing a clear reference point to decide whether any option fits. Unlike standard EBMs that only learn relative compatibility among options, ZeroPoint integrates the decision to select an option or abstain into ordinary inference, trained with negative log-likelihood loss, without requiring a separate rejection rule. The model uses a small multilingual encoder that processes the input and options invariant to their order. Experiments show that training with examples where no option fits contributes most to the model's effectiveness. ZeroPoint's fixed zero state separates inputs with and without acceptable options better than a learned rejection class and significantly better than thresholded softmax, while maintaining consistent choice among options. This approach enhances decision-making in scenarios where abstention is a valid outcome.

entry.title: Researchers propose State-Conditional Invariance for reliable vision-language model judges and introduce GridWM-Judge benchmark revealing diverse failure modes in multimodal task evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a principle requiring vision-language model (VLM) judges to maintain stable verdicts under semantics-preserving presentation changes while responding to causal task outcome changes. They introduce GridWM-Judge, a diagnostic benchmark based on MiniGrid trajectories with variants testing perception, transitions, presentation stability, and causal discrimination. Evaluations reveal varied failure modes including sensitivity to evidence presentation, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak counterfactual discrimination, with visual grounding and objective recovery identified as key model-dependent challenges. The study suggests reporting correctness alongside presentation stability and causal sensitivity for more reliable VLM judge assessments.

entry.title: Study compares three evaluation frameworks for enterprise LLM analytics agents, assessing stability, known risk detection, and unknown failure discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks-trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics-applied to two analytics agents using frozen execution traces. They found that 97% of configurations met stability thresholds, with the trace-based framework achieving the best precision-recall balance on known risk detection and text-only evaluation generating more false alarms. The study also uncovered 24 novel failures with no overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming, highlighting the complementary nature of these approaches. The results indicate that the quality of evaluation depends on the information available to the harness, and that LLM-based evaluation can detect subtle errors missed by human reviewers. The authors recommend using a two-framework strategy combining trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation to improve reliability in enterprise analytics agent deployment.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Contrastive Discovery method for LLM agents to resolve scientific questions by evaluating competing explanations, improving resolution rates across six domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Contrastive Discovery, a method that replaces single hypothesis testing with contrast sets containing mutually exclusive competing explanations, allowing large language model (LLM) agents to better resolve scientific questions. This approach scores experiments based on how evidence redistributes belief among alternatives, enabling agents to identify which explanation the evidence supports rather than just rejecting one hypothesis. In tests across six domains, Contrastive Discovery resolved 73% of rejected hypotheses to specific alternatives and increased question resolution by 67% compared to pointwise evaluation under the same experiment budget. A blinded study with 38 human experts showed high agreement with the method's resolved explanations, supporting its effectiveness in improving scientific discovery from existing evidence and validation resources.

entry.title: Researchers develop method to improve clinical documentation models by filtering actionable clinician edits to reduce hallucinations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in clinical documentation, where clinicians edit AI-generated outputs before use. Researchers found that over 45% of these edits add information not supported by the model's inputs, risking hallucinations if used for fine-tuning. To address this, they created a taxonomy of clinician editing behaviors based on real-world data and generated semi-synthetic edit data using the MIMIC-III dataset for discharge summaries. They introduced filtering methods to identify actionable edits, showing that naive fine-tuning on raw edits increases ungrounded content, while their filtering approach improves alignment with clinician expectations and maintains faithfulness to input context.

entry.title: Researchers propose Möbius Interaction Filtering for multimodal humor detection, achieving 70.6% accuracy on UR-FUNNY and demonstrating applicability to sentiment prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Möbius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), a method that jointly interprets language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior for multimodal humor detection by regulating interaction orders through spectral regularization. MoIF uses private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interactions to build unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors aggregated via a Möbius-domain filter that controls higher-order contributions to prediction. Experiments on the UR-FUNNY dataset show MoIF improves signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 to 2.79 times compared to co-trained trimodal predictors, achieving 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1, outperforming thirteen other methods. Evaluations on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI datasets confirm MoIF's applicability to sentiment prediction, with cross-seed analyses indicating more stable performance estimates. The approach links multimodal interaction organization to statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint, and the code is publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers analyze when multi-temperature sampling improves large language model inference and find single tuned temperature often suffices in pass@K settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate the effectiveness of varying sampling temperatures during inference in large language models, focusing on the pass@K evaluation setting. They analyze success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, discovering that while multi-temperature schemes can improve performance, the gains over a well-tuned single temperature are generally modest. The study identifies that harder questions tend to require different temperatures, but this effect grows only logarithmically with difficulty. The authors introduce an efficient method to evaluate optimal multi-temperature allocations and explain the limited benefits through mathematical "dulling effects" that stabilize temperature choices across question distributions. Their findings clarify when temperature diversity is beneficial and provide guidance on selecting sampling temperatures for inference.

entry.title: Researchers propose ASPIRE, a large language model agent framework for nonlinear system identification with iterative reasoning and exploration, validated on three physical systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ASPIRE is a framework that uses a large language model agent to autonomously select and execute nonlinear system identification methods, constructing interpretable models from measured data with optional physical knowledge and requirements. The system operates interactively or autonomously, allowing iterative analysis and validation, and was tested on a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter, producing valid models in all 30 runs at low cost. The evaluation showed that the models met most criteria for interpretation, structure selection, and parameter estimation, with some discrepancies related to unsupported claims about model structure selection. ASPIRE's approach aims to reduce the need for expert intervention in system identification by integrating formal verification and user interaction.

entry.title: Researchers propose action-sequence alignment using longest common subsequence to select compatible successful references for multi-turn on-policy distillation, improving performance on ALFWorld and airline benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the challenge of selecting suitable successful trajectories as references for multi-turn on-policy distillation (OPD) in tool-use agents, where incompatible successes can mislead supervision. They model reference selection as an optimal transport problem and use action-sequence alignment via longest common subsequence (LCS) to measure compatibility between failed and successful trajectories, making compatibility the key criterion for reference selection. Experiments on the ALFWorld environment and the airline domain of the \(\tau^3\)-bench demonstrate that LCS-based reference selection outperforms reference-free OPD across multiple metrics. Additionally, models trained with airline data transfer effectively to the retail domain, showing improvements without further optimization, highlighting the generalizability of the approach.

entry.title: Researchers propose sequence-level Rényi entropy from Sequential Monte Carlo decoding as a zero-cost uncertainty measure for adaptive large language model reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a method to quantify uncertainty over entire large language model (LLM) completions using sequence-level Rényi entropy (SRE) derived from Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding, enabling selective prediction and adaptive compute without additional cost. This approach extends to a family of stepwise entropies and outperforms traditional log-probability signals in multiple settings, including the MATH500 benchmark. The study demonstrates that the order-1/2 Rényi entropy accumulates per-step search effort and serves as the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in most tested scenarios. An 8-particle probe identifies tasks benefiting from more particles, and a two-pass policy achieves accuracy comparable to 64-particle decoding with 34.2% fewer particles, indicating efficiency gains in adaptive LLM reasoning.

entry.title: Researchers model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution for gaze-augmented reward training, improving preference prediction accuracy in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a method that integrates human eye-tracking data into reward model training for language models by modeling visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on gaze location. This approach builds on cognitive psychology findings about letter recognition and extends prior fixation-centric models to better align model outputs with human preferences. Their experiments show that the reward model trained with this gaze distribution achieves higher accuracy in predicting preferences compared to baseline models. Some results align qualitatively with established knowledge of human attention during reading, suggesting the model captures meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

entry.title: Synapse-Control introduces lightweight runtime control for large language model agents, improving task success by 29.8% and reducing inference costs compared to Sentry [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Synapse-Control is a new agent runtime designed to enhance the reliability of large language model agents on complex tool-based tasks by reusing execution experience more efficiently. It uses a lightweight control plane with rules and a 1.7 billion parameter classifier to select relevant advice and decide when to send it to the task-executing model, avoiding costly generative failure diagnoses. The system employs micro-contracts for reusable interface checks and a Prompt Value Table to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget constraints. In tests involving 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieved 270 successes-29.8% more than the baseline-while replacing 4,987 generative diagnosis calls and cutting auxiliary control time by about half compared to Sentry.

entry.title: Researchers assess personalized privacy protection capabilities of 21 large vision-language models using SPY-Bench, finding low compliance and limited contextual understanding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated 21 state-of-the-art large vision-language models (LVLMs) for their ability to enforce personalized privacy protections at inference time, using a new benchmark called SPY-Bench with 32,700 samples across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios. They found that most models performed poorly, with only about 24% compliance accuracy and limited understanding of contextual privacy instructions. To address this, the team developed initial alignment methods, including a Noise Contrastive Alignment variant that achieved 96.88% accuracy while maintaining general performance, marking a step toward more controllable and ethical LVLM deployment.

entry.title: Researchers introduce CAMP-II to train language-model agents on file-based memory for long-horizon tasks, achieving nearly 3x improvement over prior methods on CAMG-II environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), a method that trains a single policy across five long-horizon reinforcement learning environments to learn file-based memory behaviors using asynchronous on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher. CAMP-II enables agents to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements, significantly improving performance on the Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II) benchmark suite. The approach achieves 2.97 times the gain of the strongest previous baseline and generalizes to external benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 with improved success rates.

entry.title: Researchers build HandsOnAid, an offline 4-bit Gemma 2B language model fine-tuned on first-aid data for emergency response, evaluated with medical guidelines and LLM judges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B language model fine-tuned on a dataset of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs to assist in emergencies without phone signal or ambulance access. They tested seven model configurations using a medically reviewed question bank aligned with ANZCOR guidelines, scoring answers with a strict rubric and safety overrides. The best model, a fine-tuned 4-bit version with retrieval, scored 2.51 out of 5, with evaluations by both advanced LLM judges and a medical professional showing consistent results. A keyword audit revealed gaps in the training data coverage of some ANZCOR guideline details, likely contributing to the modest scores. On a Pixel 7 Pro smartphone without network connection, the fine-tuned model generated initial text in under 7 seconds and completed answers in under 15 seconds on average, demonstrating practical offline usability for emergency first-aid assistance.

entry.title: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.10201v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

entry.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2601.21343v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are classically trained in stages: pretraining on raw text followed by post-training for instruction following and reasoning. However, this separation creates a fundamental limitation: many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new way to pretrain and mid-train models that incorporates these behaviors earlier. We utilize an existing strong, post-trained model to both rewrite data and to judge policy model rollouts, thus introducing thinking and reinforcement earlier in training. We further improve reasoning at all stages by introducing the concept of self-improving post-thinking: improving the model's reasoning and self-judging ability by reasoning after generation. In our experiments, we show these approaches can give strong gains across multiple axes.

entry.title: Cold-Start Personalization via Bayesian Adaptive Questioning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2602.15012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cold-start personalization requires inferring preferences from minimal interaction when no user-specific historical data is available. The space of possible preferences is vast, yet users care about only a sparse subset and rarely articulate them upfront; combined with limited interaction budgets, this makes preference elicitation challenging. Our key insight is that preferences exhibit predictable structure across populations; e.g., users who want detailed explanations often also value worked examples. We propose CAPE (Cold-start Adaptive Preference Elicitation), which learns a structured world model of preference correlations offline from complete profiles, then performs training-free Bayesian inference online to select informative questions and predict complete preference profiles, including dimensions never asked about. Even simple belief model instantiations (e.g., linear regression) substantially outperform end-to-end RL. Across medical, mathematical, social, and commonsense reasoning, CAPE achieves 80.8% alignment with ground-truth user preferences versus 68.5% for RL, requires 2.5x to over 15x fewer interactions, and adapts its questions twice as often as RL. Our contribution is a principled decomposition of cold-start personalization that makes Bayesian preference elicitation practical at scale for LLM systems.

entry.title: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2605.12798v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training a language model can induce surprising behavioral changes far beyond the intended training target. We study two particularly striking examples: emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning on a narrow dataset leads to misaligned behavior in unrelated contexts, and subliminal learning (SL), where a student model inherits a teacher's misalignment through seemingly benign training data. We examine how the training data, evaluation data, and training method shape where and how strongly misalignment transfers between data and models. We characterize the data by the domain of a prompt (its topical context) and its task (the function the model performs), and we build natural-language and synthetic datasets organized as domain-task grids. We find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts that share the task of the fine-tuning data than to prompts that share its domain. In the synthetic setting, tasks that the model has learned well spread misalignment more broadly. For SL, we go beyond SFT (supervised fine-tuning) to off-policy distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution and, to our knowledge for the first time, on-policy distillation, where the teacher only scores tokens sampled by the student. Misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under SFT and at a level comparable to off-policy distillation. Unlike SFT, where the teacher both generates the data and supervises the student, distillation lets us separate the two. With the teacher fixed, the data change how much misalignment the student inherits, but the teacher determines to which domains and tasks it transfers most strongly. Together, these results show how data and training influence the extent and patterns of emergent and subliminal misalignment.

entry.title: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2605.16245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into the online platforms where humans exchange opinions; large language models (LLMs) have been polishing users' posts on LinkedIn and providing context for content shared on X. While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We address this gap via a combination of empirical and theoretical analyses. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. Building on this observation, we introduce a mathematical model of opinion dynamics in which an AI system sits between users on a social network, transforming the opinions they express and perceive. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.

entry.title: Pruning and Distilling Mixture-of-Experts into Dense Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2605.28207v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is now the dominant architecture for frontier language models, yet it requires all expert parameters to be loaded in memory, making it less preferable for memory-constrained deployment. Existing compression methods reduce the number of experts but the output remains an MoE model with the same fundamental limitation. We present the first systematic framework for converting a trained MoE into a standard fully dense architecture: experts are scored, selected, and grouped, then concatenated into a dense FFN and refined by knowledge distillation from the MoE teacher. We evaluate 7 scoring, 5 grouping, and 2 magnitude scaling methods across a range of selected expert counts on Qwen3-30B-A3B, yielding 350 configurations. We find that the choice of scoring method is the most impactful, with our novel diversity-aware scoring consistently outperforming prior methods on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and GPT-OSS-20B. Under a controlled comparison at matched parameter count, MoE-to-dense outperforms dense-to-dense pruning by +6.3 pp in average downstream accuracy after ~4B-token distillation at 1.6x faster training wall-clock speed.

entry.title: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.07537v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surveys of hallucination classify errors by how an output relates to its source, and often explain them by the model's structure: attention retrieves by association, the maximum-likelihood objective has no term for truth, and left-to-right decoding commits to early tokens. Data, on this account, makes these failures worse rather than causing them. The account is usually argued rather than tested. We test it with interventions that need only sampling access. Study 1 holds pretraining data, tokenizer and scale fixed and swaps attention for a state-space mixer, using five Pythia/Mamba pairs from 130M to 2.8B parameters and four further attention models, on 111 facts presented with a planted false or a planted true statement. Swapping the mixer leaves free-recall failure unchanged (both 2.8B models answer 3 of 200 SimpleQA questions), but it changes what happens to a defect in the input. From 410M upwards, every attention model repeats the planted falsehood more often than its matched state-space model (2.8B: 650 vs. 566 of 666 items, p = 2.5e-20), also on facts both models know, while the state-space models can still read planted facts they did not know. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models. The correct fact cuts the share of answers with a downstream error from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works as well (p = 0.38), and the models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. The structural account survives in a narrower form. The mixing component decides whether a defect in the context becomes an output error, commitment decides how an error spreads, and on long-tail questions the first error comes from missing knowledge, not from a suppressed truth.

entry.title: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2606.23700v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

entry.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.19181v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

entry.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2608.09928v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.

entry.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.36202v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love trains", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, perform far worse. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.

entry.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.06706v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

entry.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

entry.title: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.11551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.

entry.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed TopicScope, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to train causal topic classifiers capable of labeling the topic of each token in a model's generated response. Unlike previous activation-based monitors limited to detecting harmful content with few classes, TopicScope assigns topics dynamically throughout a response. Trained on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics, the classifiers demonstrated robustness to perturbations and generalized well across different model sizes. The study highlights that compact topic monitors can be efficiently trained during the prefill phase and deployed during generation, expanding the application of SAEs beyond safety classification. The associated code, dataset, and checkpoints are publicly available.

entry.title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study investigated whether large language models internally represent psychological constructs or merely produce outputs resembling psychometric patterns. Using responses from Taiwanese university students and analyzing 14 variants of Llama 3 and Qwen models, researchers found that larger models replicate and amplify human psychological scale correlations. Internal geometric structures aligned with human data were observed in larger instruct models but not in base variants. The study also identified a phenomenon termed "readout attenuation," highlighting differences between internal model activations and behavioral outputs. Overall, the findings demonstrate decodability and alignment of psychological constructs within these models under specific assays, though they do not confirm that internal representations directly mediate observed behaviors.

entry.title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study explores the application of reinforcement learning techniques to optimize cancer chemotherapy treatment schedules. The research includes simulations using traditional Q-learning and advances to offline reinforcement learning methods, employing a model-based architecture with conservative Q-learning and offline policy optimization. Utilizing real clinical data from colon cancer patients, the proposed approach aims to generate optimal sequential treatment policies. Experimental results suggest that this model can effectively support junior oncologists in making treatment decisions.

entry.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study reevaluated the performance of tabular foundation models (TFMs) against optimally tuned gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) for predicting customer churn in the telecom sector. Unlike previous benchmarks that compared TFMs to untuned GBDTs and focused solely on ranking metrics, this analysis considered profit-related metrics and calibration across five public telecom churn datasets. The results showed that the TabPFN-3.5 model achieved significantly higher expected maximum profit than the best tuned GBDTs on certain datasets, while other TFMs showed mixed results. The study also noted that licensing restrictions on TabPFN-3.5 weights currently limit its production deployment. Overall, the findings suggest that TFMs can offer advantages over tuned GBDTs in specific contexts, though further considerations such as licensing and dataset independence remain important.

entry.title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.

entry.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.

entry.title: Building World Models from Intrinsic Motivation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the absence of extrinsic rewards or task supervision, human behavior is guided by intrinsic motivation---neural signals that drive curiosity, creativity, play, and other essential facets of intelligence. Intrinsic motivation plays an important developmental role in building robust world models that enable generalization and adaptation. Yet existing studies leave open how a broad range of intrinsic motivations interacts with world-model representation learning to support downstream control. This limits our understanding of which intrinsically collected experiences build reusable models. To address these gaps, we integrate 24 intrinsic objectives, including established methods and explicit variants spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency, into a common model-based reinforcement learning framework. We evaluate the world models they build through zero-shot, few-shot, and multi-task control in locomotion, manipulation, and open-ended gaming environments, using three representation-learning strategies: observation reconstruction, latent prediction, and redundancy reduction. Curiosity-driven exploration with observation reconstruction yields the strongest aggregate family profile, although the best individual pairing depends on the experiment. In compositional vision-based tasks, intrinsic motivation derived from both episodic and lifelong novelty---providing a complementary memory to the world model's generic recurrent state---achieves the best zero-shot transfer and few-shot adaptation. These findings motivate designing intrinsic motivation and representation learning jointly. Our results demonstrate world models as a powerful tool for measuring the quality of intrinsically motivated experience, and positions intrinsic motivation as a key ingredient for building world models autonomously.

entry.title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.

entry.title: Agreeing on the Answer but Not the Reason: Measurement Limits of LLM Reasoning Failure Taxonomies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Failure taxonomies for LLM reasoning are increasingly reported as measurements: papers state what fraction of a model's errors fall into named categories, then compare those fractions across models. We show that for one such category the reported fraction is largely a property of the measurement procedure. We defined Compositional Collapse (a model notices a required sub-part of a problem, then drops or misapplies it) and measured it across twelve models and eleven languages on a public multilingual math benchmark (2,316 graded records). First, 50.1% of failures carry evidence for more than one category, so the reported plurality depends on the order in which the classifier tests them: reversing two tests moves it in eleven of twelve models, and across all six orderings Collapse's share spans 26.4% to 76.4%. Second, agreement collapses for the category but not for the task. Native speakers of all eleven languages judged 179 transcripts, agreeing with our inspector at kappa = 0.932 on answer correctness but only kappa = 0.093 on Collapse. A second native speaker per language re-rated 142 items; on 121 determinate pairs the two humans agree with each other at kappa = 0.659, while each agrees with the inspector at kappa <= 0.094. Re-running the same inspector model with the human instructions verbatim raises kappa against Human 2 from 0.147 to 0.636, so the gap is largely attributable to the prompt, not the model. Third, the inspector labels Collapse 1.81 times as often as native speakers, but only 1.17 times once a defective benchmark item (a deleted clause in the Bengali and Chinese translations) is excluded. We recommend four cheap checks before comparing failure-mode rates across models: report label co-occurrence, permute the tie-break, validate on a shared independent sample, and audit systematic disagreements.

entry.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, \$126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame before sampling, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span \$11.2-15.0B agree to within \$0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on re-draws of the design with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that charges every human label, a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by \$3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval, and institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Every headline result is re-run under each reader. The results identify both the benefits and the limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

entry.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $\tau^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

entry.title: Darmok: Championship Cryptic Crossword Solving via Constraint Tightening and Resilient Orchestration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Darmok, the first automated system to reach superhuman performance on British cryptic crosswords. Unlike American-style crosswords, cryptic clues disguise an unmarked definition and compositional wordplay beneath a misleading surface reading, sparse grids leave nearly half of each word's letters unchecked, and tournament rules rank a grid with even a single wrong or blank square behind all error-free solutions regardless of speed. Competing alongside an elite human field at the 55th Times Crossword Championship in London, Darmok solved all seven championship puzzles error-free and finished faster than every human competitor in every round. It solved the Final puzzle in 6m 52s, a full 3m 13s ahead of the human champion. Today's frontier AI models can on average solve a whole puzzle in a single try with comparable accuracy and speed. However, cloud API calls still stall, time out, trigger safety refusals, or get stuck in reasoning loops. To simultaneously achieve tournament-grade accuracy, speed, and reliability, Darmok cross-checks clues across three independent models in rounds; uses verified crossing letters to unlock harder clues; and uses a whole-puzzle model and dictionary lookups to fill any remaining gaps without overwriting confirmed words. This design maintained near-zero-error performance across a five-month daily evaluation period. Under normal benchmark conditions, removing backup models, fallback steps, or elaborate prompt instructions barely changes accuracy, making the architecture appear over-engineered. Yet during both the worst days of daily operation and a severe slowdown of our primary model in the live Championship Final, the backup paths carried the solve, showing that as foundation models master the average case, the central challenge in building complex AI systems shifts to resilience in the worst case.

entry.title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.13975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE

entry.title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($\Delta = -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($\Delta = -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.

entry.title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.

entry.title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

entry.title: Multimodal Abstention That Preserves Acquired Correct Answers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adding abstention to a task-adapted multimodal model can discard correct answers, including capabilities acquired during adaptation. We formulate abstention repair as maximizing correct abstention on unanswerable questions under a budget on newly lost correct answers. We propose ReFrain (Regression-Free Abstention), which combines a linear probe on first-token logits, threshold calibration on held-out image clusters, and a deterministic veto that replaces rejected outputs with the displayed "none of the above" option while preserving all other responses. "Regression-free" denotes zero loss on the calibration set at the zero-budget target. All abstention methods in our main comparison start from the same answering-SFT checkpoint; we separately track lost correct answers, repaired errors, and retained SFT gains. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, ReFrain at zero budget retains all 57 SFT-gained answers with no losses and improves correct abstention by 7.30 percentage points. At a 0.5% calibration budget, it reaches 74.05% correct abstention with 8 losses and retains 55 gains; CLIP-UP EmbLoRA reaches 64.65% with 62 losses, 41 repairs, and 40 retained gains. The same probe at its default threshold loses 298 correct answers. With models and thresholds frozen, confirmation on 228 independent question clusters yields 66.05% correct abstention and no losses at the 0.5% point, exceeding EmbLoRA by 32.72 percentage points. Ordinary refusal SFT achieves higher correct abstention at greater regression cost. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/ModeLiberaL/ReFrain.

entry.title: When Should Agents Remember? Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon, verifier-rich environments, but current self-improvement mechanisms often write episode-derived lessons directly into memory, making local success an unreliable signal for reusable and safe knowledge. This paper addresses the core question of when an experience-derived behavioral update should be admitted into persistent agent state. We propose Falsification-Gated Self-Evolution (FGSE), a verifier-grounded framework that represents each candidate lesson as a structured hypothesis with an explicit precondition, behavior change, expected effect, and verifier. FGSE applies the hypothesis only in a temporary state, tests it on target-transfer, falsification, and archived-regression probes, and then commits, refines, or rejects it according to measured gain and risk. Across web, app, tool-use, and long-term memory benchmarks, FGSE achieves strong task performance, including 39.8 WebArena success rate, 78.8 AppWorld average completion, and 0.724/0.487 Pass$^1$ on $\tau$-Retail/$\tau$-Airline, while reducing falsification failures to 5.0%, regression damage to 1.3%, and harmful committed updates to 3.6%. These results suggest that testing memory updates as hypotheses supports more reliable long-term adaptation.

entry.title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_\theta(x)\propto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

entry.title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

entry.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.14492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $\tau^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

entry.title: Textual Response-Aware Guidance for Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2610.40309v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing adversarial fine-tuning methods often use pre-trained model guidance to preserve image--text alignment while improving robustness. Our analysis of visual representation drift reveals complementary limitations of two representative forms of guidance. Matching visual features constrains all directions equally, providing broad coverage without semantic emphasis. Matching prediction distributions prioritizes semantically relevant directions, but remains limited by the candidate texts and prediction probabilities. These limitations can hinder preservation of pre-trained image--text relationships and degrade zero-shot performance. We therefore propose Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), which constrains visual representation drift using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. TRAG constructs anchor-level constraints from the response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image--anchor relevance, yielding an image-adaptive constraint. Extensive experiments across architectures and tasks demonstrate state-of-the-art clean and robust performance. Further analysis shows that TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image--text relationships.

entry.title: Rethinking in Spikes: Mitigating Hallucinations in MDLMs with Step-Aware Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.12901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advancements in multimodal diffusion language models (MDLMs) have exhibited strong global modeling capabilities through iterative refinement. We observe that mask uncertainty follows an overall downward trend during iterative denoising, while a few denoising steps exhibit localized entropy spikes closely associated with hallucinations.
